questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the encoded insertion point that a halving search returns when the key is absent

options.misconception: a miss reports the midpoint index where the search stopped
the encoding counts the insertion point itself with no off-by-one shift
a miss reports the number of comparisons the search performed

questions.explanation: A miss returns the bitwise complement of the insertion point, so the insertion point is 2 and the result is 2 negated then decremented, which is -3. The tempting answers read the negative value as a signalled position or as a work count, but neither is what the method documents: it hands back one number that encodes both the fact of the miss and the index at which the key would have to be inserted to keep the order.
questions.hint: Count how many entries of the sorted range sort before the key, then apply the documented negation.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the encoded insertion point for a key that sorts before every entry

options.misconception: a miss at the front reports index zero with no sign change
a miss at the front reports the count of entries that sort after the key
the front insertion point is one so the encoding is the complement of one

questions.explanation: No entry sorts before the key, so the insertion point is index 0 and the miss is reported as 0 negated then decremented, which is -1. The tempting answer picks 0 because that is the position the key would occupy, but the method never returns a bare position on a miss: it folds the miss flag and the position into one value, and a positive result would be indistinguishable from a hit.
questions.hint: Ask how many entries sort before the key, then remember the encoding shifts by one.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a halving search that is restricted to a sub-range of a sorted array

options.misconception: the bounded form still reports the index within the whole array
the bounds only slow the search down and change nothing about the result
the insertion point is counted from the start of the whole array

questions.explanation: The bounded form searches only index 5 through 6, which holds the single value 11, and 7 is absent from that window. The insertion point for a key that would sit after 11 is index 6 in absolute terms, and the miss encoding gives -6. The tempting answer 3 comes from the unbounded search, but the bounds argument changes the range under inspection, so the result describes the window rather than the array.
questions.hint: List the values actually inside the range you passed, then ignore everything else in the array.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a halving search over a range whose keys all repeat

options.misconception: a halving search always returns the first matching index it could reach
a halving search always returns the last matching index in the range
a range of identical keys is treated as a miss because no unique hit exists

questions.explanation: The search is looking for a key that is present, so it reports a non-negative index, and the index it lands on is whichever midpoint happens to be examined first. That index is not fixed by the specification, so 2 is a legitimate answer and 0 or 4 would be equally legitimate on another run. The tempting answers assume a tie-breaking rule the method does not promise, which is exactly why a program that needs the first or last match must search for it explicitly.
questions.hint: Decide only whether the result is a hit or a miss, then remember the specification does not fix which duplicate is found.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a truncation copy that asks for fewer elements than the source holds

options.misconception: the copy starts one element in so the last one is dropped
a shorter request still produces an array of the original length
a shorter request pads the front with default values and drops the rest

questions.explanation: The second argument is the length of the result, not a starting index, so the copy takes the first two entries and stops. The tempting answers confuse the length with an offset or with a minimum size, and both readings contradict the method's own contract: the new array has exactly the requested length, and when that length is larger than the source the shortfall is padded at the end with default values instead.
questions.hint: Read the second argument as a length, and ask whether the result is longer or shorter than the source.

questions.topic: Copy Of Range Pads Past The End
questions.learningObjective: trace a range copy whose end index runs past the end of the source

options.misconception: the copy starts at index zero so the leading value is kept too
the result is padded but only part of the way to the requested length
an end past the array length is silently clamped to the length

questions.explanation: The result has exactly the requested length of eight slots, so the copy takes the two values that exist from index 1 onwards and fills the remaining six with the default value for an int. The tempting answer clamps the end and returns a short array, but that belongs to a different method: this one sizes its result from the end index alone, so a too-large end produces padding rather than a shorter array.
questions.hint: The result length is decided by the end index alone, so count the slots the request asks for.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a range copy whose end index precedes its start index

options.misconception: an inverted range is reported as an out of range index
an inverted range is reported as a misuse of the list state
an inverted range leaves the result null and printing it fails

questions.explanation: A start index above the end index is a contradiction in the request rather than an index that happens to lie outside the array, and the method reports it as an illegal argument. The tempting answer picks the bounds exception because both problems involve a wrong number, but the specification separates the two cases: an index outside the array is a bounds failure, while a start above the end is an illegal argument even when every index is individually in range.
questions.hint: Both indices here are valid array positions, so the failure cannot be about a position being out of range.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze whether copying each row separately breaks aliasing between two grids

options.misconception: copying each row leaves both rows aliased to the original cells
the write reaches the original grid but the rows are still distinct
a row copy makes a second reference to the same row and no new cells

questions.explanation: Each call to the copy method allocates a new row and copies the values into it, so the two grids no longer share any row and the write to the copy cannot reach the original. The tempting answer 99 true mixes the two effects people expect, but copying the outer reference alone would leave the rows shared, whereas copying inside the loop gives every row its own storage and leaves grid[0][0] at 1.
questions.hint: Ask where the new cells are allocated, and whether the write can still find its way to the original grid.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: apply the deep comparison rules to two grids whose rows have different lengths

options.misconception: the shared prefix of the shorter row is enough to call the grids equal
a deep comparison refuses to run on rows of unequal length
a deep comparison returns null when the row lengths disagree

questions.explanation: A deep comparison checks shape as well as values, so the second row's extra cell makes the two grids different even though every value they share matches. The tempting answer stops at the matching prefix, but that is a rule about scanning for a value rather than about comparing two containers, where a length difference is itself a difference and the method reports it as a plain false.
questions.hint: Decide whether row length is part of what two grids being equal means.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze why the shallow comparison overload reports two identical looking grids as different

options.misconception: the comparison looks inside each row so matching values make the grids equal
comparing two object arrays whose rows are arrays is a type error
the comparison gives up and returns null for nested array rows

questions.explanation: The overload chosen here is the one for object arrays, and it compares the elements with reference equality, so it is comparing two row references that point at different objects. The tempting answer assumes the comparison descends into the rows, but that descent belongs to the deep variant, and a program that wants value equality for a grid has to ask for the deep comparison by name.
questions.hint: Check which comparison the compiler picked from the static types of the two arguments.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the printed form of a grid rendered by the deep printing helper

options.misconception: the renderer prints the rows without the usual spacing after commas
the renderer flattens the grid into a single row of values
the renderer prints the row objects but drops the outer brackets

questions.explanation: The deep renderer walks the array of arrays, so it opens a bracket for the outer array and another for each row, and each value is separated by a comma and a space. The tempting answer without spacing comes from hand-written printing, but the helper reuses the same element formatting as the one-dimensional version, so the spacing and the nested brackets both come for free and the row structure stays visible in the output.
questions.hint: Each nesting level of arrays contributes its own pair of brackets.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze whether two arrays holding the same values in a different order share a hash code

options.misconception: the hash code depends only on which values are present, not on their order
comparing hash codes of arrays with different orders is a type error
comparing hash codes of arrays with different orders yields null

questions.explanation: The array hash code combines the elements in index order, so swapping the two values changes the result and the two codes differ. The tempting answer assumes the code is set-like, but that would break the contract that requires equal arrays to share a code: if order did not matter for the code then two unequal arrays could collide on the same value, and a hash based container would keep both, which is not what the contract promises.
questions.hint: Ask whether the combination step could tell the two arrangements apart.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the sign returned by the lexicographic array comparison helper

options.misconception: a negative first element difference makes the result positive
the comparison only looks at the lengths of the two arrays
the result is the difference between the two disagreeing elements

questions.explanation: The leading values match, so the comparison moves to the second position, where 2 is less than 3, and the helper reports a negative value for a smaller first argument. The tempting answers confuse the sign with the size of the gap and confuse lexicographic order with set membership: the contract promises only that the result is negative, zero or positive for smaller, equal or greater, so a program must test the sign rather than the magnitude.
questions.hint: Find the first index where the two arrays disagree and ask which side is smaller there.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the index reported for the first position where two arrays disagree

options.misconception: the reported index is the length of the arrays when they differ somewhere
the reported index counts how many leading values agree in total
a reported index of minus one means the arrays have different lengths

questions.explanation: The helper scans from index 0 while the values match, and index 0 matches, so it advances once and stops at index 1 where 2 and 9 disagree. The tempting answer counts the agreeing prefix rather than the disagreeing position, and the negative answer belongs to the separate question of equal content with different lengths, which this pair does not raise because both arrays are the same length here.
questions.hint: The scan advances while the values agree, so count the agreements before the first difference.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a write made through a fixed-size list onto the array that backs it

options.misconception: the list keeps a private copy so the array is left untouched
the replacement lands on the second slot rather than the first
the replacement is written to every slot that held the old value

questions.explanation: The list produced from an array is a view, not a copy, so it holds a reference to the very same array and a replacement writes straight into it. The tempting answer assumes a defensive copy, but that assumption would defeat the purpose of the method, which exists to let existing array code and list code share one set of data; what the view refuses is changing the size, not changing a value.
questions.hint: Ask whether the list and the array can be the same storage.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace an attempt to grow a list that is a view onto an array

options.misconception: growing a fixed-size list is reported as an illegal argument
growing a fixed-size list is reported as a bad index
growing a fixed-size list is reported as a failed type conversion

questions.explanation: The view can only replace values because the array behind it has a fixed length, so a request to add an element is refused as an operation the view does not support. The tempting answers borrow exception types from other situations, but each of those reports a different problem: an illegal argument is a bad value handed in, a bad index is a position outside a range, and this is neither, it is a legal request against a view that cannot grow.
questions.hint: The request itself is well formed, so the failure must name the missing capability rather than a bad value.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Sub List Of A View Cannot Be Cleared
questions.learningObjective: analyze why clearing a sub-list of an array view fails while a sub-list of a growable list works

options.misconception: clearing a sub-list is reported as a misuse of the list state
clearing a sub-list is reported as a concurrent modification
clearing a sub-list is reported as a position outside the range

questions.explanation: Clearing a sub-list has to shift the elements that follow it and then shorten the backing list, and a view onto an array can do neither because the array length is fixed. The tempting answer blames the sub-list itself, but a sub-list of a growable list clears without complaint, so the unsupported part is inherited from the array view underneath rather than from the sub-range operation.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same clearing code would work on a sub-list of a growable list.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the runtime type produced by the parameterless array copy on a list

options.misconception: the copy inherits the element type of the list it came from
the copy returns the first element rather than a new array
the copy returns the list implementation rather than an array

questions.explanation: The parameterless copy is declared to return an array of objects, and it builds exactly that, so the runtime type is an object array no matter what the list held. The tempting answer reads the element type off the list, but the compiler has no way to promise an element type here because no target type was supplied; a program that needs a typed array must pass the type in, for example by asking for a new string array of the right length.
questions.hint: Check the declared return type of the copy that takes no argument.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze why a comparison written as a difference breaks on extreme values

options.misconception: the subtraction reports the larger value as the smaller one
the subtraction overflows into a negative value that is still not less than zero
both expressions agree that the first value is smaller than the second

questions.explanation: The comparison helper compares the values as signed quantities and reports the larger one, while the subtraction wraps around to a negative result because the true difference does not fit in an int, so the less-than test is true. The tempting answers try to reconcile the two, but that reconciliation is the whole point: a comparator written as a difference is unsound on extreme values, which is why the comparison helper exists.
questions.hint: Compute the difference on paper and check whether it fits in an int before believing the result.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a sort that breaks ties with a second comparison

options.misconception: the words are sorted by length from the longest down to the shortest
the alphabetical comparison replaces the length comparison entirely
the second comparison runs first and the length comparison only breaks ties

questions.explanation: The primary comparison decides the order, so the one-letter word comes first, the two-letter word next and the three-letter word last, and the tie-breaker never gets consulted because no two words share a length here. The tempting answers reverse the chain or treat the second comparison as a replacement, but a chained comparator only consults the next stage when the earlier one reports equality, so with distinct lengths the alphabetical rule has no effect at all.
questions.hint: Work out whether the second comparison is ever reached for this input.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a sort driven by a comparator that inverts the natural ordering

options.misconception: reversing the comparison reverses the array in place before sorting it
reversing the comparison leaves the array exactly as it was
reversing the comparison sorts by value but keeps the original order

questions.explanation: A reversed comparator reports every pair the other way round, so the sort places the largest value first and the smallest last, giving descending order. The tempting answers read reversing as a reversal of the array or as a no-op, but the comparator only decides which element is treated as smaller during the sort, and inverting that decision is exactly what turns ascending order into descending order.
questions.hint: Ask which value the sort now treats as the smallest one.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a sort whose comparator gives null values a defined position

options.misconception: nulls first places the missing value at the end of the run
the original order survives because a null cannot be compared
a null element is reported as an error by any sorting call

questions.explanation: The wrapper comparator answers the comparison for a null element itself, so the sort never asks the string comparison about null and the null lands at the front by the rule the wrapper supplies. The tempting answers assume the underlying comparison is reached for every pair, but that is exactly the failure the wrapper exists to prevent, since the string comparison would have nothing to call on a missing value.
questions.hint: Ask whether the null value ever reaches the natural string comparison.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a sort that relies on the natural ordering of a type with a missing element

options.misconception: a missing element is reported as a failed type conversion
a missing element is reported as a misuse of the sort state
a missing element is reported as an illegal argument to the sort

questions.explanation: With no comparator the sort compares elements by asking one to compare itself to the other, and a missing value has no comparison to give, so the attempt to call it fails. The tempting answers borrow exception types from type and state problems, but this is neither: the arguments are correctly typed and the array is a legal array, and the failure comes from reaching through a reference that points at nothing.
questions.hint: Ask which value the natural comparison tries to ask a question of.

questions.learningObjective: trace the position a not-a-number value takes in a sorted double array

options.misconception: a not-a-number value sorts before every other value
a not-a-number value is treated as the smallest value
a not-a-number value sorts before every other value

questions.explanation: The ordering used for doubles defines every comparison against a not-a-number value to be greater, so the real values are put in order first and the not-a-number value is pushed to the far end. The tempting answers place it first or in the middle, and a programmer who reads not-a-number as a very small or very large magnitude expects one of those positions, but the rule is defined on the comparison itself and it always sends that value last.
questions.hint: Ask how the ordering rule answers the question of whether a not-a-number is greater than a real value.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate how the comparison helpers order the two representations of zero

options.misconception: the first array is reported as greater because negative zero is below zero
the two representations of zero compare as the same value
the result is the numeric difference between the two representations

questions.explanation: The comparison helper orders the raw bit patterns rather than the numeric magnitudes, and the pattern for negative zero is defined to come first, so the result is negative. The tempting answer 0 comes from arithmetic intuition that the two values are both zero, but the numeric equality test and the ordering used here answer different questions, and a program that wants numeric equality has to ask for it separately.
questions.hint: Decide whether the comparison looks at the stored bits or at the numeric value they denote.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze why storing a value of the wrong runtime type into a widened array reference fails

options.misconception: the wrong stored value is reported as a failed type conversion
the wrong stored value is reported as a missing reference
the wrong stored value is reported as an illegal argument

questions.explanation: Widening the reference type is allowed at compile time, but every write is still checked against the component type the array was actually created with, and storing an integer into a string array breaks that promise at run time. The tempting answer names the conversion failure, but no conversion is attempted here at all, because the array is not converting the value, it is refusing it, and the refusal is reported as a bad store.
questions.hint: Ask what the array promises about its elements and which promise the write breaks.

questions.learningObjective: trace the runtime type produced by cloning an array through a broader reference

options.misconception: the copy takes the type of the reference it was assigned to
the copy collapses to the single element the array holds
the copy gets its own runtime type named after the clone method

questions.explanation: A clone of an array is the same kind of array as the original, so the copy is a string array even though a broader reference is used to hold it, which is why the method can be called through the broad type and still return something precise. The tempting answer follows the static type of the variable, but the runtime type travels with the object, and a program that widens the reference has not changed what the object is.
questions.hint: Ask whether the object changes kind when the reference used to reach it is widened.

questions.learningObjective: trace the length of an original array after a shorter copy is taken from it

both references end up pointing at the one shorter array
the copy is padded back out to the length of the original

questions.explanation: The copy allocates a new array whose length is the number that was asked for, and the original array is untouched, so the two lengths differ. The tempting answers treat the copy as an in-place operation, but an array's length is fixed at creation and no method can resize one, which is the very reason a copy has to be a separate array in the first place.

an unassigned reference slot holds the numeric zero like a primitive slot
an unassigned reference slot holds a blank but present string

questions.explanation: Every element of a newly allocated array receives the default value for its type, and the default value for a reference type is no reference at all, which prints as null. questions.topic: Fill With A Half Open Range

options.misconception: a ranged fill still covers the whole array
the range arguments are one-based positions rather than indices
the range end index is included in the fill along with the start

questions.explanation: The range form treats the arguments as a half-open interval, so it fills indices 1, 2 and 3 and leaves index 0 and index 4 holding the default value. questions.learningObjective: trace a fill whose value for each slot is computed from its index

the index function is applied once and the result is repeated
the index function receives the stored value rather than the index

questions.explanation: The index function is handed each index from zero up to the length and its result is stored in that same slot, so the first slot gets the function of zero and the last slot gets the function of three. questions.learningObjective: analyze a bulk copy whose source and destination ranges overlap

an overlapping copy is refused so the array is left unchanged
the copy runs backwards from the end and shifts the other way

questions.explanation: The bulk copy behaves as if the values were first lifted out and then put back, so the overlapping case produces the same result as copying between separate arrays: the first value is written into both slot 0 and slot 1 and the rest follow. a negative length is reported as an index outside the array
a negative length is reported as a failure to obtain memory

questions.explanation: A negative length is not an index and not an argument to a method that validates its input, it is a request for storage that cannot exist, and the runtime reports it with a name that says exactly that. questions.learningObjective: trace a read through a grid whose rows were declared but never allocated

reading a row that was never filled in is a misuse of the grid state
reading a row that was never filled in is a negative size problem

questions.learningObjective: trace the maximum of a stream whose source array has no elements

an empty maximum is reported as a numeric operation failure
an empty maximum is reported as a missing optional value

questions.explanation: The maximum of nothing does not exist, so the stream hands back an empty optional and the call that demands a value from it fails with the name that says there was nothing to take. questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: analyze what a stream total does when the true total no longer fits in an int

options.misconception: the total is reported exactly even though it does not fit in an int
the total is reported one less than the wrapped value
the total is silently clamped to the largest int it can hold

questions.explanation: The stream adds with int arithmetic, so the single value past the maximum wraps to the most negative int, which is what gets printed. The tempting answers hope for exactness or for saturation, but neither is offered: the operation is ordinary int addition run n times, and a program that needs a total beyond the int range has to widen the element type before summing rather than widening afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what the addition itself does when it passes the largest representable value.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a row-wise total computed by mapping each row to its own sum

options.misconception: the longer row contributes only as many values as the shortest row
the totals are the first value of each row rather than the whole row
the row totals are placed in the order the rows are longest first

questions.explanation: Each row becomes an independent stream of its own values, so the first row totals three and the second totals twelve, and the results keep the order of the rows. The tempting answers impose a rectangular shape that this grid does not have, but the mapping visits each row separately and never pads one row to match another, which is exactly why ragged input needs no special handling here.
questions.hint: Ask how many values each row actually contains before totalling it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace a single total taken across every cell of a grid in one pass

options.misconception: the grid is treated as a rectangle padded out to the widest row
only the first row contributes to the grand total
the total leaves out the cell at the last position

questions.explanation: Flattening turns the grid into a single stream of the four values one, two, three and four, and their total is ten. The tempting answers add a phantom cell or drop a row, but flattening visits each row exactly as long as it is and adds nothing, so the total is simply the sum of every value that is actually present in the grid.
questions.hint: Add up the values that are really there before believing any of the options.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace the array type produced when a stream of primitives is boxed on its way out

options.misconception: boxing a primitive still yields an array of the broad reference type
boxing is undone on the way out so the array holds primitives again
the array takes the type of the common supertype of the boxed values

questions.explanation: The type argument handed to the array builder is the array type to create, so a builder for an integer array produces an integer array and the boxed values are written into it. The tempting answers assume boxing degrades the type or that it is undone later, but boxing is a one-way conversion made so the values can travel through the reference-based parts of the stream pipeline, and the array type is decided by the builder, not by the stream.
questions.hint: Ask which array type the builder passed to the call is asked to create.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: trace an edit to a character array that is then turned back into a string

options.misconception: a string is immutable so editing the character array cannot be seen
the rebuild uppercases every character it copies across
the rebuild converts the letter into the character that follows it

questions.explanation: A string is immutable, so editing it is impossible, and the character array is the standard way around that: the array is writable, and building a fresh string from it afterwards produces the edited text with only the changed character different. The tempting answer carries the immutability rule one step too far, but the immutability belongs to the string, not to the array that was extracted from it.
questions.hint: Ask which object the edit was applied to and whether that object is the immutable one.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a loop whose bound lets it read one element past the end of the array

options.text: for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) { total += values[i]; }
for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) { total += values[i]; }
options.misconception: the loop should stop one step after the last element is read

options.text: for (int i = 0; i < values.length - 1; i++) { total += values[i]; }
options.misconception: the last element should be left out of a total over the whole array

options.text: for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) { total += values[i]; }
options.misconception: the loop should start one element in so the first value is skipped

questions.explanation: Indices run from zero to one less than the length, so the loop must stop as soon as the index reaches the length, and every value is then added exactly once for a total of twenty-seven. The tempting answer keeps the inclusive bound and so asks for one element past the end, while the two shortened versions quietly drop data, and all three of those are wrong in different ways from the crash the program actually shows.
questions.hint: Ask what the largest valid index is and whether the loop is allowed to reach it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a total that is replaced on every pass instead of accumulating

options.misconception: the accumulator only needs the current value because the caller adds it up
the loop counts the values as well as totalling them
the loop discounts the first value it sees

questions.explanation: An accumulator has to carry the running total forward, so each pass adds the current value to what was already collected and the final sum is two plus four plus six, which is twelve. The tempting assignment discards the running total on every pass and so reports only the last value, which is the symptom the program shows, and the two arithmetic variants are wrong because they adjust the total by a constant that has nothing to do with the values being added.
questions.hint: Ask what the accumulator held before this pass and whether that work is being kept.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a halving search whose input was never put in the order the search requires

options.misconception: sorting the caller's array is the same as sorting the copy that is searched
copying the range again is what puts the values in the order the search needs
filling the copy with ones is what makes the search find the key

questions.explanation: A halving search is only justified when the range is ordered by the key it compares, so the fix has to establish that order before searching, and a copy keeps the caller's array untouched while the search runs against ordered values. The tempting answers try to fix the problem by hiding it: sorting in place can work but corrupts the caller's data, and copying without ordering changes nothing at all, so the search still discards halves on no evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which precondition of the search is currently missing and how to supply it without damaging the input.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a fill whose two range arguments are in the wrong order

options.misconception: the range arguments may be given in either order
the range should begin at the first slot rather than the second
the range should end one slot past the last one wanted

questions.explanation: The range form takes a half-open interval, so a start of 1 and an end of 4 covers exactly the three middle slots and leaves the outer two at their default value. The tempting answer swaps the arguments, but a start above the end is a contradiction rather than a request to fill backwards, so the call is refused instead of doing something; the two shifted versions fill the wrong three slots and so produce a different array rather than a crash.
questions.hint: Ask which three indices the interval is meant to cover and in which order those two numbers are given.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a grid copy that leaves the new rows pointing at the original cells

options.misconception: assigning the row is enough because the new array already has its own storage
a shorter row copy is enough as long as the first cell is copied
allocating a fresh row is enough without copying any values across

questions.explanation: The copy is only independent when each new row holds its own freshly allocated cells, and the copy call does both the allocation and the transfer of values, which is why the original keeps its own 1 while the copy shows the edited 99. The tempting assignment gives the copy the very same row, the shorter copy leaves the second row the wrong length, and a bare allocation gives the right shape with the wrong values, and none of the three is what the caller asked for.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate row objects the finished copy needs and where their values come from.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a comparison that returns the difference of two values and so overflows

options.misconception: subtracting in the other order produces the ascending order
negating the comparison result produces the ascending order
ordering the values as text is a safe stand-in for ordering them as numbers

questions.explanation: A comparison has to report the order of two values without being able to represent their difference, and the comparison helper does exactly that, so the ages come out ascending every time. The tempting subtraction answers share the same defect, because subtracting two large values can wrap around and report the opposite order, and negating a subtraction inherits that defect too; comparing magnitudes looks safe but answers a different question, since it treats a large negative value as small.
questions.hint: Ask whether the difference of two values of this type can always be represented.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: In Place Transpose Needs A Temporary
questions.learningObjective: repair an in-place transpose that loses a value during the swap

options.text: int t = grid[r][c]; grid[r][c] = grid[c][r]; grid[c][r] = t;

options.misconception: the third assignment is unnecessary because the two cells already hold each other's values
the first assignment should store into the mirrored cell rather than the current one
adding the two mirrored values is what puts the transposed value in place

questions.explanation: The two mirrored cells are the only places the values live, so one of them has to be saved before the first write overwrites it, and the saved value then goes into the other cell, which is the classic three-step swap. The tempting answer drops the final write and so duplicates one value while losing another, the second version writes a value into the cell it just read and so changes nothing, and adding the two values answers a sum rather than a transpose.
questions.hint: Ask which cell holds a value after the first write has already destroyed it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: repair a copy loop that reads from the wrong offset in the source array

options.misconception: the offset should be one so the second value is the first copied
reading the tail backwards is the same as reading it forwards from the right offset
no offset is needed because both arrays start at the same place

questions.explanation: The tail begins at index 2, so the loop counter has to be shifted by two to reach it, and the three iterations then read 3, 4 and 5 in order. The tempting answers shift by one and so start copying one element too early, read the same three values in reverse order, which is a different array even though it holds the same numbers, and apply no shift at all, which copies the head instead of the tail.
questions.hint: Ask which index of the source holds the first value the new array should contain.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: complete a largest-value tracker that seeds itself from the first element

options.misconception: the tracker should keep whatever it already holds
the value stored should be one below the value that won the comparison
the value stored should always be the final element of the array

questions.explanation: The comparison has already established that the current value is larger than everything seen so far, so storing the current value is what advances the running maximum, and by the end the tracker holds 9. The tempting answers store something other than the winning value, and a tracker seeded from the first element has no sentinel and no separate search, so whatever is stored on a winning pass becomes the best value for the rest of the loop.
questions.hint: Ask which value just won the comparison, and where the tracker should read from next time.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: complete the body that adds a value only when it passes a two-part test

options.misconception: the accumulator should be replaced by the value that passed the test
the accumulator should count how many values passed the test
the accumulator should be scaled by the value that passed the test

questions.explanation: The guard has already decided that this value belongs in the total, so the body has to add the value to what has been collected so far, giving two plus four plus six, which is twelve. The tempting answers replace the running total instead of extending it, count matches rather than totalling them, or multiply the running total, and each of those changes the meaning of the variable from a sum into something the name and the question never promised.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value that passed the test should join the total or replace it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Counting Cells In A Ragged Grid
questions.learningObjective: complete the accumulator that totals the cells of a grid whose rows differ in length

options.misconception: the running count is not needed because every row is the same width
one cell is added for each row regardless of how wide the row is
the running count is widened by the number of rows in the grid

questions.explanation: Each pass handles one row and that row contributes as many cells as it has slots, so adding the row's length to the running count gives two, then three, then one, for a total of six. The tempting answers all use a quantity that ignores how wide a row actually is, and a ragged grid is exactly the case that punishes that: the first row has two cells and the second has three, so any single fixed width would be wrong for at least one of them.
questions.hint: Ask how many cells this particular row contributes, rather than how many rows there are.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: complete the tracker that keeps the second largest value seen so far

options.misconception: the second place should keep whatever it already holds
the second place should be given the current largest value
the second place should be one below the value that was just seen

questions.explanation: The branch is only reached for a value that is below the largest but above nothing else yet, so the second place has to keep whichever of its current value and this one is larger, which leaves 7 once the loop has passed the 9 and the 7. The tempting answers overwrite rather than compare, and overwriting is exactly the mistake the first branch already avoids, because a later small value would drag the second place down below an earlier better candidate.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value just seen is better or worse than what the second place already holds.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: evaluate which comparison expression stays correct on the extremes of the int range

options.misconception: the difference of two ints is always a correct comparison result
asking which value is smaller is the same as asking which is larger
unboxing the values before subtracting removes the overflow risk

questions.explanation: A comparison only has to say which of two values comes first, and the comparison helper says that without ever forming the difference, so the most negative value correctly ends up at the front. The tempting subtraction answers form a difference that no int can hold when the values sit at opposite ends of the range, so the sign comes out backwards and the sort reports the opposite order; unboxing changes nothing because the overflow happens in the subtraction, not in the values.
questions.hint: Ask what the difference of the most negative and most positive int actually computes.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: count the element comparisons a halving search performs before it gives up
questions.explanation: The first midpoint is index 2 holding 5, which is below the key, so the search keeps the right half and the second midpoint is index 3 holding 7, which is above the key, so the search keeps the left half of that and the range becomes empty. Two midpoints were examined and therefore two comparisons were made, which is the point of halving: the range went from five entries to none in two steps rather than five.
questions.hint: Follow the two half-range updates and count the midpoints examined on the way.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: count the pairs of positions whose values are out of ascending order
questions.explanation: The leading 5 is larger than all four values after it, the 3 is larger than the 2 and the 1, the 4 is larger than the 2 and the 1, and the 2 is larger than the 1, so the count is four plus two plus two plus one. This same count is exactly the number of shifts an insertion sort performs on this input, which is why nearly ordered data is cheap for that sort and fully reversed data is its worst case.
questions.hint: Count the values that sit after each value and are smaller than it, then add the counts up.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state the rule that fixes an array's length at the moment it is created
questions.stem: A program stores a new array reference and then wants to make that array hold one more element. Which statement about an array's length is correct?

options.text: The length is fixed when the array is created, because no operation can resize an existing array
The length grows by itself when a value is stored past the last index, as a list would
options.misconception: an array grows automatically to accept a store past its last index

options.text: The length can be shortened by assigning a new number to the length field of the array
options.misconception: the length field is a writable slot that controls how many slots exist

options.text: The length counts the distinct values stored so far rather than the number of allocated slots
options.misconception: the length reports how many different values are in the array, not its size

questions.explanation: The length is part of the array object and is set by the allocation, and the runtime offers no operation that changes it, so growing an array means allocating a new one and copying. The tempting answers come from list experience, where adding an element does work and where a size field can shrink, and both habits are wrong here: a store past the end is a bounds failure rather than a silent growth, and the length describes slots rather than contents.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is any method whose job would be to change an array's length.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: distinguish reference comparison of arrays from element-wise comparison
questions.stem: A program holds two separately built arrays with identical contents and compares them with the equality operator. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The operator compares references, while the array equality method compares element by element
Both forms compare element by element, so the operator also reports content equality
options.misconception: the operator walks the elements just as the array method does

options.text: The operator compares element by element, while the array method compares references
options.misconception: the operator looks inside the arrays and the method looks at the references

options.text: Neither form can ever report two separately created arrays as matching in content
options.misconception: no comparison of arrays can ever find two of them equal

questions.explanation: An array is an object, so the operator asks whether two references point at the same object, and two separately built arrays never do, while the array equality method is specified to walk the elements and compare them one by one. The tempting answer transfers the method's behaviour to the operator, which is the classic confusion when moving between objects and their contents; the third answer swaps the two roles entirely, and the fourth denies a capability the library plainly provides.
questions.hint: Ask whether the operator has any way to look inside the arrays at all.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Why A View Replaces But Not Grows
questions.learningObjective: explain why a list built from an array allows replacement but refuses addition
questions.stem: A list was created from an existing array. Replacing one of its elements works, but adding a new element is refused. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Replacing a value leaves the array the same length, while adding would need a longer array than the view can ever have
Replacing a value works because the view copies on write, while adding is simply never permitted
options.misconception: the view makes a private copy whenever an element is replaced

options.text: Replacing a value works because the view owns its storage, while adding is refused for lack of space
options.misconception: the view holds its own array and is simply full

options.text: Both operations are permitted, but an added element past the end is silently discarded
options.misconception: an element that does not fit is quietly dropped rather than refused

questions.explanation: The list is a window onto an array whose length was decided when that array was created, so overwriting a slot is within its powers while making it longer is not something the window can arrange. The tempting copy-on-write answer is contradicted by the visible effect, since a replacement shows up in the original array, and the ownership answer contradicts the same observation, since a view that owned storage would not be tracking the array at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether a replacement is visible in the original array, and what that says about who owns the storage.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state the hashing obligation that two equal arrays must meet
questions.stem: Arrays are to be used as keys in a hash-based container so that two arrays with equal contents can be found for one another. Which requirement must hold?

options.text: Arrays with equal contents must report the same hash code, since a container narrows candidates by code before comparing
Arrays with equal contents may report different hash codes, because the container rechecks with equality anyway
options.misconception: a container can fall back on equality even when the codes disagree

options.text: Arrays with equal contents must be the same reference, or no container will match them at all
options.misconception: only the very same array object can ever be found in a container

options.text: The hash code of an array is fixed at creation, so mutating the array cannot change the code it reports
options.misconception: a container keeps working correctly after an array used as a key is mutated

questions.explanation: A hash-based container uses the code to decide which bucket to look in and only then compares candidates for equality, so two equal arrays that reported different codes would be filed in different buckets and never meet, which is why equal contents must imply the same code. The tempting answer assumes the equality recheck can rescue a mismatch, but the recheck only ever happens between candidates already in the same bucket, and the mutation answer describes a situation in which the key is no longer equal to itself.
questions.hint: Ask at which step the container decides which stored keys are worth comparing at all.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: recognize that a varargs parameter is an array parameter with a shorter call syntax
questions.stem: A method is declared as static int total(int... values). Which statement about calling it is correct?

options.text: The parameter is an int array, so a caller may pass the values separately or hand over one int array
The parameter is a distinct kind of argument, so the values can never be passed as a single array
options.misconception: a varargs parameter rejects an array and only accepts loose values

options.text: A varargs parameter takes loose values only, and a plain array parameter takes a whole array only
options.misconception: the two parameter forms accept completely disjoint sets of calls

options.text: Both forms accept the same calls, but only the array form lets the method change the caller's array
options.misconception: a varargs method works on a private copy while an array method works on the caller's own array

questions.explanation: Writing the parameter with three dots is only shorthand for declaring an array parameter, and the compiler builds the array from the loose values at the call site, which is why an array can be handed over directly instead. The tempting answers read the dots as a new kind of parameter, but there is no extra type and no extra storage: a varargs method that changes the array it receives changes the very array the caller passed in, exactly as an array parameter would.
questions.hint: Ask what the declared type of the parameter is once the dots are read as shorthand.
